newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Czech trade gap widens, analysts wary on '97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Czech trade gap widens, analysts wary on '97.

text.p: The Czech August trade deficit widened to 14.7 billion crowns ($547.7 million) from about 10 billion crowns last year, pushing the eight-month deficit to a record 100.9 billion crowns, the Statistical Bureau said on Wednesday.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, admitting the deficit was high, said he would call a special meeting on October 8 to discuss ways to remedy the widening trade gap.

"This figure is high, and I asked five members of the cabinet to prepare analytical materials on this and materials with certain possible proposals on what to do with (the trade deficit)," Klaus told reporters after a cabinet meeting.
The government has repeatedly ruled out a devaluation of the Czech crown to boost exports, but Klaus did not say what measures might be proposed at the meeting of ministers.
Klaus's spokesman said the industry and trade, finance, and agriculture ministers, central bank governor, and statistical bureau chairman would join Klaus in the trade meeting.

Analysts said the yawning gap was followed the prevailing trends. The foreign exchange market showed little reaction, as the Czech crown firmed slightly against its mark/dollar basket immediately following the release of the trade results.
The economists said the trade deficit could be financed this year, but might pose problems in the second half of 1997.

Kamil Janacek, chief economist at Komercni Banka, said the eight-month figures -- up from a 59.5 billion crown deficit for the same period last year -- projected to a 1996 current account deficit of six percent of gross domestic product.
He said the merchandise trade deficit would be softened by a growing surplus in services, including tourism.

"The growing surplus in services will be higher by about $300 million over 1995" when the net service balance was in surplus $1.85 billion, Janacek said. The first-half services balance showed a $910 million surplus.

Still Janacek said he expected the still-strong crown to ease below parity against its mark/dollar basket from its Wednesday level of 2.8 percent above the peg, as trade and political concerns over a spate of banking failures linger.

"(The crown) will go back in the next months toward its central parity point (versus the basket)," Janacek said. "My estimate is that it will fluctuate around parity or in the depreciation interval in the first quarter of next year."

In late afternoon trading the crown was at 26.845 to the dollar and 17.768 to the mark, implying a deviation of 2.79 percent over the central bank's mark/dollar basket, after Wednesday's fixing of 2.8 percent above the basket.

Economist Vladimir Kreidl at Prague's Patria Finance said Wednesday's results implied a full-year trade deficit projected to 150-160 billion crowns. This could be financed this year, but might be troublesome next year.

Kreidl said the effects of a recovery of demand in western Europe had yet to show up in the Czech trade figures, as import growth was exceeding export growth by about 15 percent versus just over two percent over the last three months.
"We are still waiting to see whether the recovery in western Europe will change the picture," he said, adding that the stronger Czech crown was still stifling exports.
The government and central bank however has repeatedly ruled out a devaluation of the crown to boost exports.
Analysts point to mid-1997 as a crucial time in which the import wave -- which is aimed at modernising industries -- must show results in productivity growth and competitiveness.
